title: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born
hook: a prison at midnight, a river that parts, and a baby carried across it to safety

segments.voice: Last time: the driver, Krishna holding the reins for Arjuna, and the close of the stories camp. Your line was you know these people now. Today, the driver's first night. Day seventy-eight.

We left Krishna as a grown man holding a chariot's reins. Tonight's festival goes back to the very start. A prison cell in the city of Mathura. Midnight. A storm outside. A mother, Devaki, and a father, Vasudeva, in chains. Her brother, the tyrant king Kamsa, was told at her wedding that her eighth child would kill him. So he locked them up and took every baby they had. Now the eighth is coming. And the whole story of the night is one question: can a newborn be carried out of a locked prison, across a flooding river, before morning?
screen: `A PRISON AT MIDNIGHT.` → `KAMSA FEARS THE EIGHTH CHILD.` → `CAN A BABY GET OUT BY MORNING?`

segments.voice: Here's how the Bhagavata Purana tells it. At midnight, the baby is born. The guards fall into a deep sleep. The chains fall from Vasudeva's wrists. The prison doors swing open on their own. Vasudeva puts his newborn son in a basket on his head and walks out into the storm, to the river Yamuna, which is in flood. And the river, in the story, lets him through: in a popular telling, the water rises to touch the baby's feet, then parts. The great serpent Shesha rises behind him and spreads his many hoods over the basket like an umbrella against the rain. On the far side, in the village of Gokul, the cowherd's wife Yashoda has just given birth to a daughter. Vasudeva quietly swaps the babies and walks back to his cell. The doors close. The chains return. In the morning Kamsa comes for the child, and the baby girl slips from his hands, rises into the sky as a goddess, and tells him: the one you fear is already born, somewhere else. So Krishna grows up hidden among cowherds, a mischievous boy stealing butter. That's Janmashtami: janma, birth, and ashtami, the eighth day of the moon's dark half, when tradition says he was born. Households that keep the festival fast all day and stay up until midnight, singing, and at the hour of the birth they ring bells and rock a tiny cradle. In the Gita, Krishna says he comes, age after age, whenever goodness declines. Janmashtami is the night people celebrate that promise: the good doesn't always arrive at noon. Sometimes it comes at midnight, in the dark, carried through a storm.
screen: `THE CHAINS FALL, THE DOORS OPEN.` · `THE RIVER PARTS; THE SERPENT SHELTERS.` · `A BABY SWAPPED IN GOKUL.` · `JANMA + ASHTAMI: BIRTH ON THE EIGHTH.`

segments.voice: Dim the lights if you can, or close your eyes. Sit in the dark for a moment. Think of something good you're waiting for, something that hasn't come yet. Healing, a reconciliation, a job, a change in someone you love. Let the waiting be here, in the dark, the way the family waited in the cell. Now picture a single small light appearing. The door opening, just a crack. You don't have to force it. Just wait in the dark, knowing the good sometimes arrives at midnight. The bell holds the time.
Janmashtami. Janma, birth; ashtami, the eighth day. The midnight birthday of Krishna.
Your line: the good arrives at midnight. Tonight, before you sleep, sit in the dark for one breath and name one good thing you're still waiting for. Day seventy-eight.

howItsDone: On Janmashtami many Hindus fast until midnight, sing devotional songs, and at the hour of Krishna's birth ring bells and rock a small cradle holding an image of baby Krishna; in Maharashtra the next day, teams form human pyramids to break a pot of curds hung high, as Krishna the butter thief would.

original.note: Sanskrit: janma (birth) + ashtami (the eighth day of a lunar fortnight).

trapdoor: what you thought: Krishna's birthday party.
what it means: a baby carried out of a locked prison and across a flood at midnight, and a promise that the good comes in the dark.
what a scholar hears: janma + ashtami. the birth story is told in the Bhagavata Purana's tenth book; the Gita (4:7–8) gives the promise of return.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.1–10.4 (Kamsa, Devaki and Vasudeva; Krishna's birth; the crossing to Gokul; Yogamaya)
